content: Hepatitis B is a liver disease that can be prevented through vaccination. The hepatitis B virus (HBV) is present in the blood and bodily fluids of individuals who are infected. People infected with HBV can transmit the virus to others. You can contract hepatitis B through the following ways: Engaging in sexual activity with an infected partner. Sharing needles, syringes, or drug preparation equipment with someone who is infected. Using personal care items such as razors, toothbrushes, or medical devices like glucose monitors that have been used by an infected person. Experiencing a needlestick injury or being cut with a sharp object in a healthcare setting. Coming into contact with the blood or open sores of an infected individual. Transmission from an infected mother to her baby during pregnancy or childbirth. Early symptoms of hepatitis B may include fever, fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dark-colored urine, pale or clay-colored stools, joint pain, and jaundice (a yellowing of the skin or eyes). In some cases, hepatitis B can progress to a chronic infection. Chronic hepatitis B can lead to severe long-term health complications, including liver disease and liver cancer, which may result in premature death. Hepatitis B is found worldwide but is more prevalent in certain regions, including parts of Asia, Africa, South America, and the Caribbean. The most effective way to protect yourself from hepatitis B is through vaccination. In the United States, the hepatitis B vaccine is routinely administered to infants at birth. The vaccine has been recommended for infants since 1991 and is over 90% effective. The vaccination series typically consists of 2, 3, or 4 doses, which are usually completed by the age of 6 months. The hepatitis B vaccine is recommended for all unvaccinated travelers under the age of 60. It is also recommended for travelers aged 60 and older who are visiting countries where hepatitis B is common. The vaccine is administered in either 2 or 3 doses. If you are planning to travel internationally within the next 6 months, it is important to consult your healthcare provider about accelerated vaccination options. These include the 2-dose series (Heplisav-B) or an accelerated dosing schedule for the combination hepatitis A and hepatitis B vaccine.
